facts.fact: Certified exam: one day, three separate sections: Deductive Tasting, Theory/Business of the Sommelier, and a Hospitality and Service Practical. Expected skill set includes 'Deductive Tasting Method ability for core classic red and white varieties'.
Exam-day schedule lists the Tasting Examination first (8:15 AM), before Theory (8:50 AM) and Service (from 10:00 AM).
A candidate must achieve 60 percent or higher on EACH exam section; all three portions must be passed at the same exam.
Tasting exam: four wines, two whites and two reds, to identify in 45 minutes using the CMS-A Deductive Tasting Method. Candidates may not touch the glasses until given permission.

Candidates get a blank paper copy of the Certified grid for each wine, but the exam must be completed on Examplify on the candidate's own device. Suggested system: enter color, fruit, non-fruit and structure on paper; transfer to Examplify; enter the Conclusion and Sales Pitch into Examplify.

Candidates track their own time; an approximate 'Half Time' and '5 minutes' notice is given; there is no extra time to input; at 45 minutes the exam submits automatically; answers must be in Examplify to receive credit.
The wine in your glass is what you have for the exam; there is no topping up.
The 45 minutes allows about 11 minutes per wine; you should be done with the white wines by the halfway point; leave a few moments to review that every question is answered.

There are no deductions on the tasting exam, only points accumulated, and there are points for every single line on the grid. For yes/no descriptors you must check yes or no; examiners cannot assume 'no' when a descriptor is not apparent.
Six grape varieties are listed to choose from on the actual exam; the list changes depending on the exam. Candidates are responsible for naming the country of origin.

Pitfall: candidates often fail even when they get the wines correct because they do not fill in all the boxes. Fill out every line, even if it is a No. Only write descriptors or a reason where prompted; keep answers short.

Answer YES only if very apparent and key to a wine's identity, otherwise NO. Example: a Gewurztraminer may have some apple/pear, but tropical is very apparent and key, so 'No' for apple/pear and 'Yes' for tropical with descriptors such as pineapple, mango, banana.
Choose one answer per line for every line, except Fruit Condition, where you may choose up to two.

Review before choosing a grape: does the description match the conclusion? If you called the wine off-dry and chose Sauvignon Blanc, look back for where things went off-track. Look at structure and trust structure; it is a significant indicator of certain grape varieties.
Prep advice: practice explaining why it is the grape you chose with specific fruit, non-fruit and structure reasons; for climate, look at fruit condition and structure.

Prep advice: taste examples of all Certified examinable grapes and regions and practice writing out full grids; compare wines, paying attention to fruit condition and structure (sweetness, tannin, acidity, alcohol).

Suggested comparisons, whites: Vouvray and German Riesling; Chablis and Sancerre; California Chardonnay, Chablis and oaked Cote d'Or Chardonnay; Pinot Grigio and Chablis; Gewurztraminer and Torrontes; New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc and Sancerre; Albarino and Pinot Grigio.

Suggested comparisons, reds: Burgundy and US Pinot Noir; Burgundy Pinot Noir and Nebbiolo; Sangiovese and Nebbiolo; Sangiovese and Rioja; French Grenache and Rioja; Bordeaux and California Cabernet Sauvignon; Australian Shiraz, Argentine Malbec and California Zinfandel.
White grid color line: Straw, Yellow, Gold. Red grid: Purple, Ruby, Garnet.
White grid fruit lines: Apple/Pear, Citrus, Stone Fruit, Tropical; red grid: Red, Black, Blue. Each is Yes/No; if Yes, provide one specific fruit; if No, write 'None'.
Fruit condition is asked separately for the nose and the palate; choices Tart, Ripe, Overripe, Jammy, Candied, Baked, Dried, Bruised; select one or two.
Non-fruit descriptors combine nose and palate; select Yes only if it is an important character of the wine, No if not; one answer per line, no blank lines.

White non-fruit lines (12): Flowers; Fresh Herbs, Hay; Green Bell Pepper, Grass, Jalapeno, Asparagus; Grape Variety Spice: Allspice, Pepper, Cardamom; Noble Rot/Botrytis: Ginger, Honey, Saffron, Wax; Oxidation: Nuts, Dried Fruit; Lees: Dough, Baked Bread, Yeast, Beer, Cheese Rind; Malolactic Fermentation: Butter, Cream, Yogurt; Petrol, Gasoline, Rubber; Earth: Wet Leaves, Mushroom, Compost; Mineral: Mineral, Wet Rock, Sulfur; New Oak: Vanilla, Toast, Smoke, Cinnamon, Nutmeg, Clove.

Red non-fruit lines (13): Flowers; Fresh Herbs, Tomato Leaf; Dried Herbs; Green Bell Pepper, Grass, Jalapeno, Asparagus; Mint, Eucalyptus; Black Peppercorn; Coffee, Cocoa, Mocha; Meat, Blood, Leather; Balsamic, Tar; Carbonic Maceration; Earth: Forest Floor, Wet Leaves, Mushrooms, Compost; Mineral: Mineral, Wet Rock, Sulfur; New Oak: Vanilla, Smoke, Toast, Coconut, Dill.
White structure: Phenolic Bitterness (Yes/No); Sweetness (Dry, Off-Dry); Acidity and Alcohol (Low to Medium-, Medium, Medium+, High). Red structure: Tannin, Acidity, Alcohol on the same scale.

Conclusion: Primary Grape Variety (select from examinable varieties); Climate (Cool, Moderate, Warm); Country of Origin; Age Range (white 1-2, 3-4, 5+ years; red 1-3, 4-6, 7+ years); 'Sell this wine to a guest in two sentences or less.'

Feedback report categories for each color: Visual (Primary Color); Nose & Palate (Fruit: Type; Fruit Condition: Nose; Fruit Condition: Palate; Non-Fruit); Structure (whites: Alcohol, Acid, Phenolics, Sweetness; reds: Acidity, Alcohol, Tannin); Conclusion (Country of Origin, Climate, Climate Reasoning, Grape Variety, Grape Variety Reasoning, Vintage, Guest Sales Pitch).

Conclusions guide, grape: give specific reasons from your description; review what stands out most and what makes the wine unique; apply grape variety markers, structure matches, grape growing and winemaking.

Conclusions guide, climate (cool, moderate, warm): look at fruit condition and structural elements such as acidity and alcohol; do your structure calls match the grape and where it is grown; is there a change from the nose to the palate?
Conclusions guide, country: do the structure calls match the grape, and do the grapes match these countries? Connect wine law and where grapes are typically grown.
Conclusions guide, age: look at fruit condition, color or lack of it, focus on fruit or savory elements, and any sediment.
Advanced and Master final conclusion adds region and appellation, official quality level and vintage to grape and country.

Example filled-out red grid in the exam guide: reasons 'Black fruit, black pepper, eucalyptus' and 'High alcohol, very ripe fruit'; country Australia; red fruit lines filled with blueberry, blackberry and black cherry.

'What Makes a Wine Classic?' by Shayn Bjornholm, MS, Examination Director, CMS-A (mentoring session). Quoted definition (Steve Poe, MS): a classic wine sets a distinctive offering against which all other wines from the same variety are judged.
Classic criteria questions: is its flavor profile unique and distinctive; does it have an established quality level; does it have global market presence?

If a wine does not check 'yes' for all of the qualification boxes, it does not qualify for the CMS deductive tasting examination. One box asks whether the region's wine shows unique and similar characteristics in all but the most idiosyncratic vintages.
Wayne Belding, MS (quoted): Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc, Argentine Malbec and Torrontes, and Aussie Shiraz have risen from non-existent to classic in a few decades.
Mia Van de Water, MS (quoted): taste a range of producers in every region; tasting only one producer teaches you that producer, not the region.

Original vs modern: original Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon: pyrazines, moderate-plus alcohol and astringent tannins, fruit just ripe, oak not as forward. Modern: pyrazines more subtle, high alcohol and rounder tannins, fruit overripe/liqueur-like, oak more forward.
As white wines age they become more yellow and brown; red wines lose color and become more transparent.
Nebbiolo and Grenache often show a garnet or orange rim even when young; Malbec often has a magenta rim.
Tannin is the drying, sandpaper-like feel on the tongue in red wines.
Riesling often shows a striking aroma similar to petrol or petroleum wax, from a natural compound called TDN.
Methoxypyrazines (IBMP) cause the herbaceous bell-pepper character of Cabernet Franc and are also found in Sauvignon Blanc; Cabernet Sauvignon shares the trait.

Carbonic maceration: uncrushed grapes are placed in a sealed vat and topped with carbon dioxide; such wines have low tannin and color, juicy fruit and bold yeast aromas; common with entry-level Beaujolais.
The Court's examinable list gives Gamay from Beaujolais 'with carbonic maceration' and no oak, and Rioja Reserva or Gran Reserva with American oak.
Oak lactone gives woody, dill and coconut notes; European oak is denser and has been suggested to impart less oak lactone than American oak.
Wine Folly taste profile, Riesling: off-dry, light body, high acidity, under 10% ABV.
Wine Folly taste profile, Gewurztraminer: low acidity, 13.5-15% ABV.
Wine Folly taste profile, Nebbiolo: high tannins, medium-high acidity.
Wine Folly taste profile, Pinot Noir: low tannins.
Wine Folly taste profile, Zinfandel: over 15% ABV.

The exam guide's prep page still asks 'Why is it from a particular world of origin?' while the grid asks for a country. This chapter follows the grid.
The feedback report lists a 'Vintage' item under Conclusion; the grid itself calls the line 'Age Range'. We treat them as the same line.
Links from grid lines to grapes (petrol to Riesling, pyrazines to Sauvignon Blanc and the Cabernets, oak lactone to American oak) come from Wine Folly, not the Court.

read.stopsTitle: Three habits that protect your score

stops.name: Tick No
stops.text: If a note isn't there, tick **No** (and write **None** on a fruit line). Examiners can't assume a blank means No.

stops.name: Yes means key
stops.text: Tick **Yes** only if the note is **very apparent and key** to the wine's identity. A Gewurztraminer may hint at apple, but **tropical** fruit is what defines it.

stops.name: Keep it short
stops.text: Choose **one** answer per line, except **fruit condition**, where up to **two** are allowed. Write descriptors or reasons only where the grid asks.

read.where: From Level 1: the color and fruit choices. At Certified level, the Court's feedback scores **primary color**, **fruit type**, and **fruit condition** on the **nose** and on the **palate** as separate items. Treat each one as its own answer.

stops.name: Primary color
stops.text: Whites: **straw**, **yellow** or **gold**. Reds: **purple**, **ruby** or **garnet**. Whites deepen toward yellow and brown with age; reds lose color.

stops.name: Fruit families
stops.text: Whites: **apple/pear**, **citrus**, **stone fruit**, **tropical**. Reds: **red**, **black**, **blue**. On Yes, name **one specific fruit**; on No, write **None**.

stops.name: Fruit condition
stops.text: Pick one or two of **tart, ripe, overripe, jammy, candied, baked, dried, bruised**. The Court asks whether the condition **changes from nose to palate**; that feeds your climate call.

read.mixup: **Fruit type** is the fruit you name. **Fruit condition** is its state: tart, ripe, jammy, dried.

read.where: From Level 1: tannin is the drying feel on your tongue. At Certified level you place acidity, alcohol and tannin on a **four-step scale**: low to medium-minus, medium, medium-plus, high. The Court's advice is short: **look at structure and trust structure**.

stops.name: White wines
stops.text: **Phenolic bitterness** (Yes or No), **sweetness** (**dry** or **off-dry** only), **acidity** and **alcohol**.

stops.name: Red wines
stops.text: **Tannin**, **acidity** and **alcohol**. There's no sweetness line on the red grid.

stops.name: The cross-check
stops.text: If your notes say **off-dry** and your answer says **Sauvignon Blanc**, the Court suggests looking back for where things went off-track.

read.mixup: **Phenolic bitterness** is scored on whites. **Tannin** is scored on reds.

read.bigIdea: Reason from your notes, then sell the wine.
read.where: The conclusion asks for a **primary grape**, **climate**, **country of origin** and **age range**, then a **sales pitch**. The Court's feedback scores **grape reasoning** and **climate reasoning** apart from the answers, so the why earns points too.
read.stopsTitle: How the Court says to reason

stops.name: Grape
stops.text: Name the markers that make the wine unique and check the structure fits. You choose from **six grapes** listed on the exam.

stops.name: Climate
stops.text: Read **fruit condition**, **acidity** and **alcohol**. Does the fruit change from nose to palate?

stops.name: Country
stops.text: Ask whether the grape fits the country and the structure fits both. Wine law and where grapes grow are your tools.

stops.name: Age
stops.text: Weigh **fruit condition**, **color**, a **fruit or savory** focus, and any **sediment**.

read.mixup: **Climate reasoning** uses fruit condition and structure. **Grape reasoning** uses the markers that make the wine unique.

read.bigIdea: Classic wines are the benchmarks you're tested on.
read.where: In a Court mentoring session, the Court's Examination Director asks three questions of any wine: is its profile **unique and distinctive**, does it have an **established quality level**, and does it have **global market presence**? A wine has to tick **every** qualification box to be used in deductive tasting.

stops.name: Original vs modern
stops.text: Some classic regions have a second style. The session contrasts an original Napa Cabernet (**pyrazines**, fruit just ripe) with a modern one (**higher alcohol**, riper fruit, more oak).

stops.name: New classics
stops.text: **Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc**, **Argentine Malbec and Torrontés** and **Australian Shiraz** became classics in a few decades.

stops.name: How to practice
stops.text: Taste every examinable grape and region, and write full grids. Taste a **range of producers**, then compare look-alikes like **Chablis and Sancerre**.
